content: 1. Cervical cancer mortality reduction is analyzed in relation to the number of precancer treatments in the general population. Women who test positive are treated based on their eligibility determined by Visual Inspection with Acetic Acid (VIA). Women who are triage-positive are referred for colposcopy, and those who remain triage-positive after VIA are treated accordingly. Women positive for HPV types 16/18 are treated only if they are also triage-positive via VIA. It is important to note that some women may require multiple treatments due to follow-up needs. 2. In scenarios where HPV testing is conducted every 5 years for women aged 30-50, or every 10 years for women aged 35-45, the cost-effectiveness of these strategies is evaluated in terms of cost per health-adjusted life year (HALY). All positive women are treated based on VIA eligibility, and triage-positive women are referred for colposcopy. Women positive for HPV types 16/18 are treated only if they are also triage-positive via VIA. Multiple treatments may be necessary for women requiring follow-up. 3. Summary tables provide outcomes over the lifetime of a cohort of 100,000 women. These outcomes include cervical cancer cases, cervical cancer deaths, precancer treatments, additional preterm deliveries due to excisional treatments, the number needed to treat (NNT) to avert a cervical cancer death, and discounted lifetime costs. The percentage reductions in cervical cancer cases and deaths are compared to no screening, while differences in precancer treatments, NNT, and costs are compared to baseline scenarios. 4. For women undergoing HPV testing at 12 and 24 months after a positive primary screening test, minimal changes in cervical cancer incidence and mortality are observed when using HPV 16/18 genotyping or colposcopy for triage. These approaches result in fewer treatments, improved NNT, and lower costs. However, when VIA or cytology is used for triage, there is some loss in overall effectiveness, but substantial reductions in harms and costs are still achieved. 5. When triage-negative women return for HPV testing at 24 months instead of 12 months, there is a potential loss in effectiveness for VIA or cytology triage. For HPV 16/18 genotyping, this delay may reduce the number of precancer treatments with only a minor loss in effectiveness. 6. The WHO suggests that women in the general population who test positive on an HPV primary screening test and are triage-negative with HPV 16/18 genotyping or colposcopy should be re-tested with HPV at 24 months, if feasible. If the follow-up HPV test is negative, these women can return to the regular screening interval.
